paragraphs.heading: What luminosity measures
paragraphs.text: Luminosity is the total power that a light-giving object sends out: how much electromagnetic energy leaves it in each unit of time. In astronomy the word is used for stars, galaxies and other glowing objects in space. In SI units it is given in joules per second, which are the same thing as watts. Astronomers also often use the Sun's own luminosity, written L_(☉), as a unit.

paragraphs.heading: Not the same as brightness
paragraphs.text: Luminosity is an absolute measure of what the object gives off, not of how bright it looks. When astronomers say brightness, they usually mean apparent brightness: what an observer actually sees. That depends on three things together: the object's luminosity, its distance from the observer, and how much of its light is absorbed along the way. Apparent magnitude is a scale for apparent brightness that works by logarithms.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring the whole output
paragraphs.text: On its own, the word luminosity means bolometric luminosity, given either in watts or in solar luminosities. The IAU has set a nominal solar luminosity of 3.828×10²⁶ W so that published figures can be compared. On Earth, a bolometer measures radiant energy by absorbing it and tracking how much it heats up, but it is not sensitive enough across the spectrum to use on a star. Instead, astronomers measure a star at a few wavelengths and build a mathematical model of the full spectrum that best fits those readings. Sometimes this takes a long leap, with a luminosity worked out when under 1% of the energy is actually seen.

paragraphs.heading: Size and temperature
paragraphs.text: A star's luminosity can be worked out from two of its properties: its size and its effective temperature. Size is usually given in solar radii, R_(☉), and temperature in kelvins, yet usually neither one can be measured directly. Finding the radius needs two more numbers, the star's angular diameter and how far it is from Earth, and for most stars one or both are far too small to measure with any certainty. Effective temperature is just the temperature of a black body that would give the same luminosity, and it is estimated from the star's spectrum.

paragraphs.heading: The distance route
paragraphs.text: Another way is to measure how bright the star looks and how far away it is. A third ingredient is then needed: extinction, the dimming caused by gas and dust between the stars, in Earth's atmosphere and around the star itself. Getting each of these pieces right is one of the central challenges of astronomy. Extinction can be measured directly only when both the true and the observed luminosity are known, but it can be estimated from the star's colour, using models of how much the interstellar medium reddens light.

paragraphs.heading: Why stars differ so much
paragraphs.text: Stars are classed by temperature, from Class O stars above 30,000 K down to Class M stars below 3,500 K. Luminosity is proportional to temperature to the fourth power, so this spread in temperature turns into a far wider spread in luminosity. Luminosity also depends on a high power of a star's mass, which is why massive, luminous stars live much shorter lives. The most luminous stars are always young, no more than a few million years old in the most extreme cases.

paragraphs.heading: Big is not always brightest
paragraphs.text: Size and temperature together lead to some surprises. Deneb has a luminosity around 200,000 L_(☉) and a temperature around 8,500 K, giving a radius of about 203 R_(☉). Betelgeuse has a luminosity around 100,000 L_(☉) but is far cooler, around 3,500 K, so its radius is about 1,000 R_(☉). Red supergiants like Betelgeuse are the largest stars, yet the most luminous stars are much smaller and hotter. R136a1, for example, is over 46,000 K and more than 6,100,000 L_(☉), but its radius is only 39 R_(☉).
